results.corrected_extracted: Gastrointestinal effects in 36 (51%): vomiting 31, nausea alone 5. Tachycardia in 27 (38%; no threshold stated) and systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg in 32 (45%). Median stay 16 hours (IQR 11.3–24.4; range 1.8–228). Eight (11%), all of whom had taken tramadol with another medicine, went to intensive care: 5 for the other medicines' toxicity (tricyclic antidepressants 3, morphine 1, atenolol 1) and 3 for respiratory depression (one intubated, one on a naloxone infusion, one who developed pneumonia). No deaths. Naloxone was given to 9, seven with documented respiratory depression: it was reported to improve oxygen saturation or consciousness in 6, to improve them partly in 2 and to have no effect in 1; no seizures were reported after it.
results.note: Every number matches. Wording only: the paper says naloxone 'was reported to improve' (response taken from the medical record, Methods 4th paragraph) and that one ICU patient 'developed pneumonia'.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors say serotonin toxicity reported after therapeutic use or overdose of tramadol has been with other medicines given with it, particularly serotonergic antidepressants (1st paragraph); later they say the majority of reported cases involved co-ingested serotonergic drugs and only one unusual severe case has been described (5th paragraph). Their concluding paragraph takes the absence of serotonin toxicity in these overdoses as suggesting that at therapeutic doses tramadol is unlikely to cause more than minor serotonergic effects, although nobody taking therapeutic doses, alone or with antidepressants, was studied.

results.corrected_extracted: 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, the two sites earlier DIMS monitoring found most active on ecstasy tablets; collected by hand, with each report's stated content, physical description, picture and date archived. DIMS employees compared each report with DIMS database records (GC–MS composition, physical characteristics, date and place of submission) of the tablet within 12 weeks before or after the report's date. Stated MDMA was scored too high or too low if more than 10 mg from the database value (for a range, its average); 'unreported substance' if similar database tablets in the window held substances the report did not mention; 'dangerous' if stated more than 40 mg too low (for a range, its average 40 mg too low or its maximum 40 mg below the database maximum) or if an unreported substance was psychoactive and present in relevant concentrations (not defined in numbers). The comparison rested only on the report's own information, so a poorly described tablet matched several distinct database tablets ('multiple database hits'), which the authors take to mean that several pills on the market fitted the description and a reader could not tell them apart from the report. All four authors list the Trimbos Institute as an affiliation, and the scoring was done by DIMS employees; the paper does not state who runs DIMS.
results.note: Every methods detail and number matches pp. 94-96. Only the last sentence changed: the paper does not say that the Trimbos Institute runs DIMS (only reference 5's garbled 'Trimbos DIMS Jaarbericht' hints at it).
Table 1 (300 dpi) and the Results paragraph match every value, including 10.6 mg (6.7-14.4) and chi-square 10.86; 100 - 39.7 - 17.6 = 42.7.

Recomputed independently: 312, 159 and 72 from Table 1; only 34/159 against 38/312 gives Pearson chi-square 6.890; ratio 1.76, odds ratio 1.96 (1/0.511 = 1.96). Printed P 0.007 equals a one-sided Fisher exact test (0.0071).

The three definitions are worded as stated (abstract p. 94, methods p. 96, discussion p. 98); overstatements judged 'too speculative'; the abstract's omitted-spread wording is not a methods criterion.

Matches both Discussion paragraphs and reference 15 (Cole et al. 2002). Detail: the dealer explanation is introduced as a hypothesis often seen on the websites themselves; the explanations 'cannot be validated by the current data'.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors call this, to their knowledge, the first study of how reliable online information on ecstasy content is; they say people in the Netherlands are arguably better informed about drug content than elsewhere because of DIMS, and that extrapolating abroad needs care. They tried to score each report's source (experience, home test, laboratory test) and gave up: reports often named no source, and where DIMS laboratory tests were named as the source the stated amounts were frequently not found in the database (no numbers given). Declaration of interests: none.
results.note: Everything else matches p. 99; the hedge 'To our knowledge' is restored.

results.corrected_extracted: National Poison Data System records of reports by members of the public and health-care providers to US poison centres, most commonly collected and coded by Specialists in Poison Information; forensic testing to confirm the reported exposure is not routinely performed. Retrieved: all intentional single-agent exposures to 11 designer benzodiazepines (adinazolam, clonazolam, cloniprazepam, diclazepam, etizolam, flubromazepam, flubromazolam, meclonazepam, nifoxipam, norflurazepam, pyrazolam), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2017, all routes; accidental ingestions and exposures to more than one substance excluded. Etizolam had been tracked since 2007, but specific codes for all the other agents were added only in 2016; agents without a specific code could not be retrieved.
results.note: Everything matches Methods paragraphs 1-2; only the qualifier is restored: data are 'most commonly' collected and coded by Specialists in Poison Information.
Results 1st paragraph also gives the 330% ((112-26)/26 = 331%). Tables 1 and 2 and the footnote match at 300 dpi; agents add to 234; 201 + 32 = 233 (one sex missing).

key_findings.correction: Median length of stay 16 hours (IQR 11.3–24.4, range 1.8–228); 19.9 hours (IQR 13.6–35.7) after co-ingestion. 8 patients (11%), all of whom had taken other medicines, went to intensive care: 5 for co-ingestant toxicity (tricyclic antidepressants 3, morphine 1, atenolol 1) and 3 for respiratory depression (one intubated, one on a naloxone infusion, one who developed pneumonia). No deaths. Naloxone was given to 9 patients, 7 with documented respiratory depression; it was reported to improve oxygen saturation or consciousness in 6, to improve them partly in 2 and to have no effect in 1; no seizures were reported after naloxone.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The amount comparison between patients with and without seizures is given p=0.018 in the Results (p. 3) and p=0.021 in the Figure 1 legend (p. 4). | consequence: Minor; the direction is unaffected. The paper does not explain the difference, which may be a transcription error or a different computation (for example exact against approximate Mann–Whitney p).

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate fits: complete prospective case capture and pre-defined outcomes, against one centre, self-reported amounts without laboratory confirmation, 72% co-ingestion and few events. Design (case series) and instrument (JBI prevalence) also agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: frequencies are reported faithfully; the title's 'causes' and the conclusion's extension to therapeutic doses (hedged 'suggesting') sit at the upper end of minor.

missed: Figure 1 (PDF p. 4), measured on a 600-dpi rendering: the no-seizure group's central bar sits at about 1,400 mg with whiskers at about 350 and 2,470 mg, not at the text's median 1,000 mg (IQR 775–1,550 mg), although the legend says the bars are median and IQR; a figure–text inconsistency (the seizure group's centre, about 2,100 mg, matches).

The authors' stated hypothesis was that serotonin toxicity would occur with tramadol overdose and that seizures and coma would be the most important effects (PDF p. 2, Introduction, last paragraph); the serotonin finding ran against their own hypothesis.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract's conclusion that patients also prescribed stimulants or opioids should be monitored for benzodiazepine misuse does not match Table 2, where, among people who used benzodiazepines, prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse (AOR 0.69, 0.57–0.84) and prescribed stimulant use was not significantly associated with it (AOR 0.90, 0.74–1.09); the associations were with misuse and abuse or dependence of those drugs. (Prescribed opioid and stimulant use did go with higher odds of any benzodiazepine use: AOR 2.54 and 2.11, Table 1.) | consequence: Cite the associations with opioid and stimulant misuse and use disorders, not with prescribed use.

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate fits (national probability sample, design-based analysis; self-report, frame exclusions, no response rates). Design and instrument agreed. Small point: Table 3 has 26 rows but 25 tests (none for theft from a health care setting).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, at its upper end. In 'claimed', prescribed stimulant use (AOR 0.90, 0.74-1.09) is better described as not significantly associated than as 'no difference'.

missed: Table 1 (PDF p. 4): adjusted for the other characteristics, the odds ratio for any use is higher at 65 or older (AOR 2.28, 2.04–2.54) than at 50–64 (AOR 2.04, 1.86–2.22), both against 18–25, so the statement that use at 50–64 exceeds use at 65 or older rests on crude prevalences only (14.3% against 12.9%).

key_findings.correction: For errors in the stated MDMA amount, only understatements (more than 40 mg too low) were scored as dangerous: the authors considered whether reports overstating MDMA by more than 40 mg should also count, judged that risk too speculative to score, and so left the commonest error (overstatement) out of 'dangerous'. (An unreported psychoactive substance could also make a report dangerous.)

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate fits: laboratory-based reference, but unknown denominators, unblinded scorers without reliability data, undefined 'relevant concentrations' and several misprinted statistics. Recomputed: all Table 1 counts are consistent; Table 4 P values are one-sided Fisher (0.472, 0.007, 0.417 reproduce).

missed: The card's affiliations note (p. 94) and where_it_stands say the Trimbos Institute, or the authors' team, runs DIMS; the paper does not state this. It says only that all four authors are at the Trimbos Institute and that the scoring was done by DIMS employees (p. 95).

The Results use causal verbs for cross-sectional associations: including a picture 'leads to' better tablet recognition (p. 96), and spread inclusion 'causes a significant difference' in dangerous scoring (p. 97).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The text gives coma as 8% and agitation/irritability as 14% (Results, 2nd paragraph), while Table 3 gives 10 (4%) and 22 (9%) of 234. | consequence: Use the table's counts; the text percentages are those of the table's hypotension (8%) and confusion (14%) rows, not of coma or agitation.

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate for the description of reported, coded single-agent exposures, with the card's own caveat that it is weak evidence of what a named agent does. Design (registry) and instrument agreed. Recomputed: outcome denominators about 229 (etizolam about 158, clonazolam 49), as the card says.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, at its upper end: the headline 330% and 'incidence' mix reports with the 2016 coding change (etizolam alone 26 to 60), which the authors admit only among the limitations.

missed: Discussion, 5th paragraph (PDF pp. 5–6), the authors' counterpoint on agent identity: in three US case reports, LC–MS confirmed etizolam, flubromazolam and clonazolam, so testing verified the suspected agent in all case reports they reviewed; in a Georgia cluster of 11 impaired drivers, phenazepam was confirmed in all and at least one other drug in 6 of 11.
